title: Case 1: Cardiology - Acute Coronary Syndrome Discharge Summary
clinical_note:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY
PATIENT: 58-year-old male
ADMISSION DIAGNOSIS: Acute coronary syndrome, rule out myocardial infarction.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
Patient presented to the Emergency Department complaining of acute substernal chest pressure radiating to the left shoulder and jaw, accompanied by diaphoresis and dyspnea on minimal exertion. Symptoms commenced approximately 3 hours prior to presentation.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION & DIAGNOSTICS:
Vital signs: BP 154/92 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, SpO2 97% on room air.
Cardiovascular: S1/S2 present, regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Normal jugular venous pressure.
Laboratory: Serial cardiac biomarkers showed initial troponin I at 0.04 ng/mL, peaking at 0.82 ng/mL at 6 hours post-admission, consistent with non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI). Serum creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, baseline eGFR >60 mL/min.
Electrocardiogram (ECG): Normal sinus rhythm with 1.5mm ST-segment depressions and T-wave inversions in anterolateral leads (V4-V6).
Echocardiography: Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) estimated at 50% with mild anterolateral wall hypokinesis.

HOSPITAL COURSE:
Patient was admitted to telemetry and placed on therapeutic anticoagulation with enoxaparin. Diagnostic coronary angiography via right radial approach revealed 80% stenosis in the mid-left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery. Successfully underwent percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with deployment of a single drug-eluting stent (DES). Post-procedure course was uneventful without hemostatic complications at access site.

DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS:
1. Aspirin 81 mg PO daily (lifetime)
2. Clopidogrel 75 mg PO daily (dual antiplatelet therapy for 12 months minimum)
3. Atorvastatin 80 mg PO qhs (high-intensity lipid-lowering therapy)
4. Metoprolol succinate 25 mg PO daily (titrate to resting HR 60-70 bpm)
5. Sublingual nitroglycerin 0.4 mg PRN for recurrent chest pain

FOLLOW-UP & INSTRUCTIONS:
Follow-up appointment scheduled at outpatient Cardiology clinic in 2 weeks. Comprehensive metabolic panel and lipid panel repeat in 6 weeks. Cardiac rehabilitation referral placed. Patient instructed to seek immediate emergency medical care if experiencing recurrent retrosternal chest pain unrelieved by 1 sublingual nitroglycerin tablet within 5 minutes.
Missing/Omitted details: Specific outpatient cardiologist name not designated in note.

title: Case 2: Neurology - Intractable Migraine with Visual Aura
clinical_note:
CLINICAL ENCOUNTER NOTE
SPECIALTY: Outpatient Neurology
PATIENT: 34-year-old female
CHIEF COMPLAINT: Refractory episodic hemicranial headache with photophobia.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
Patient presents with a 4-day history of escalating severe right-sided pulsatile cephalalgia (rated 8/10 on visual analog scale). Headache is preceded by scintillating scotomas and transient left-sided homonymous hemianopsia lasting approximately 30 minutes. Accompanied by severe phonophobia, photophobia, intractable nausea, and two episodes of bilious emesis. Patient reports taking over-the-counter NSAIDs (ibuprofen 800mg) and acetaminophen with caffeine without sustained analgesic relief.

NEUROLOGICAL EXAMINATION:
Mental status alert and oriented x4. Cranial nerves II through XII grossly intact. Fundoscopic examination shows sharp optic disc margins bilaterally without papilledema. Sensation intact to light touch. Deep tendon reflexes 2+ symmetrical throughout. Negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs. Gait is steady; Romberg negative.

DIAGNOSTIC IMAGING:
MRI Brain with and without gadolinium contrast: Normal brain parenchyma. No acute ischemic stroke, intracranial hemorrhage, parenchymal mass lesion, or abnormal meningeal enhancement.

ASSESSMENT:
Intractable episodic migraine with typical visual aura, without status migrainosus. Evidence of medication overuse component secondary to frequent OTC analgesics.

PLAN & THERAPEUTICS:
1. Sumatriptan 50 mg PO at onset of migraine headache phase; may repeat dose once after 2 hours if headache persists (max 200 mg in 24 hours). Contraindicated in ischemic coronary disease.
2. Ondansetron 4 mg ODT PRN nausea/emesis every 8 hours.
3. Preventive therapy: Initiate Topiramate 25 mg PO daily at bedtime, titrating upward weekly by 25 mg to a target maintenance dose of 50 mg BID.
4. Discontinue daily combined OTC analgesics to treat medication overuse headache.

DISCHARGE / DISPOSITION:
Maintain daily headache symptom diary logging triggers, duration, and abortive medication frequency. Return to neurology clinic in 6 weeks. Seek immediate emergency evaluation for 'thunderclap' sudden-onset headache or focal neurological deficits.
Note: Specific daily sodium intake restrictions were not evaluated or documented.

title: Case 3: Pulmonology - Community-Acquired Pneumonia with Hypoxia
clinical_note:
INPATIENT PROGRESS NOTE
SPECIALTY: Internal Medicine / Pulmonology
PATIENT: 66-year-old female
ADMISSION DIAGNOSIS: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), acute hypoxemic respiratory failure.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
Patient presented with a 5-day history of progressive dyspnea, chills, nocturnal diaphoresis, and a productive cough yielding thick mucopurulent greenish sputum. Associated with right-sided pleuritic chest pain aggravated by deep inspiration. Past medical history notable for moderate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD, GOLD stage II) and 35 pack-year tobacco use.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:
Vital signs: Temp 38.8 C (101.8 F), BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 102 bpm (tachycardia), RR 26 breaths/min (tachypnea), SpO2 89% on ambient air, correcting to 94% on 2 L/min via nasal cannula.
Pulmonary: Coarse crackles (crepitations) and bronchial breath sounds auscultated over the right lower lung base. Dullness to percussion over right posterior hemithorax. Egophony positive at right lung base.

DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP:
1. CBC: Leukocytosis with WBC count 15.4 x 10^3/uL, 84% neutrophils with left shift (bandemia 6%).
2. Serum Lactate: 1.6 mmol/L (within normal limits).
3. Sputum Gram stain: Gram-positive diplococci suggestive of Streptococcus pneumoniae; culture and sensitivities pending.
4. Chest Radiograph (CXR): Dense alveolar consolidation in the right lower lobe with visible air bronchograms. Trace right parapneumonic effusion, no pneumothorax.

ASSESSMENT:
1. Severe Community-Acquired Bacterial Pneumonia (CURB-65 score = 2: tachypnea, age >= 65).
2. Acute exacerbation of COPD secondary to pulmonary parenchymal infection.
3. Mild hypoxemic respiratory insufficiency, oxygen-responsive.

MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Ceftriaxone 1 g IV every 24 hours.
2. Azithromycin 500 mg IV every 24 hours (atypical coverage).
3. Supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula titrated to maintain SpO2 between 90-94% (avoid hyperoxia in COPD).
4. Inhaled Duoneb (Albuterol 2.5 mg / Ipratropium bromide 0.5 mg) nebulized every 6 hours PRN wheezing or dyspnea.
5. Prednisone 40 mg PO daily for 5-day course for COPD flare.
6. Incentive spirometry 10 breaths every hour while awake.

FOLLOW-UP / NEXT STEPS:
Inpatient telemetry monitoring. Reassess sputum culture results at 48 hours for antibiotic de-escalation. Repeat chest radiography prior to discharge. Outpatient pulmonology appointment in 4 weeks. Note: Outpatient antibiotic oral step-down choice will be determined upon culture finalization.
